d: Application binary interface: the description of a contract’s functions and events that apps use to call it.
Ethereum keeps a balance and storage per account, like a bank account.
A 20-byte identifier derived from a public key (EOA) or assigned at deployment (contract).
Automated market maker: a pool that prices trades with a formula instead of an order book.
A third party in an escrow who can release or refund the payment in a dispute.
A signed statement by an address about something, for example a document hash (EAS).
A batch of transactions with a timestamp and the hash of the previous block.
A system that locks tokens on one chain and issues a representation on another.
The rules by which nodes agree on one order of transactions.
Code that runs once when a contract is deployed; its arguments are filled in at deployment.
Decentralised autonomous organisation: a group whose rules and treasury are run by smart contracts.
A web app whose important rules and money live in smart contracts.
Decentralised finance: exchanges, lending and stablecoins built from smart contracts.
Ethereum Improvement Proposal: the public process for changing the protocol.
Externally owned account: an account controlled by a private key; the only kind that can start a transaction.
The standard interface for fungible tokens.
The standard interface for non-fungible tokens, each with a unique ID.
A log entry a contract emits; apps and explorers read it, contracts cannot.
Ethereum Virtual Machine: runs contract bytecode identically on every node.
A website that gives free test ETH for a test network.
The point after which a block cannot be reverted; on Ethereum about two epochs.
A loan borrowed and repaid within one transaction, without collateral.
A split in rules or history. Soft forks tighten rules; hard forks require everyone to upgrade.
A test that runs a rule with many random inputs.
The unit of computation on Ethereum; the fee is gas used times gas price.
A fixed-length fingerprint of any data. Ethereum uses Keccak-256.
A storage network that addresses files by their content hash.
A network that executes transactions off Ethereum and settles on it, such as a rollup.
A tree of hashes whose root commits to every item; proofs need only a few hashes.
Maximal extractable value: profit from choosing the order of transactions.
The EU Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, fully applicable since 30 December 2024.
Reusable code in Solidity that runs before or after a function, often for access control.
The address that called the current function.
A wallet that needs several signatures, for example 2 of 3, to move funds.
A computer that stores the chain and checks every block.
A service that brings outside data into a smart contract.
A Solidity keyword that lets a function receive ETH.
Consensus in which validators lock ETH and lose part of it if they cheat.
A contract that forwards calls to a replaceable implementation, making upgrades possible.
12 or 24 words that recreate every key in a wallet. Never share it.
A bug where a contract is called back before it updates its state.
A failed transaction: all its changes are undone, but the gas is paid.
A legal text and code linked by a hash.
A Layer 2 that posts transaction data and proofs to Ethereum.
The Ethereum test network for applications, used in this course.
A program on a blockchain that holds state and funds and runs when called.
A legally binding contract in which code defines or performs some obligations.
A token designed to keep a stable value, usually one US dollar or euro.
A model in which a contract is always in exactly one state and moves between states by rules.
A delay between approving and executing an action, giving users time to react.
Unspent transaction output: Bitcoin’s model of coins, like individual banknotes.
The smallest unit of ether: 1 ether is 10^18 wei.
A proof that a statement is true that reveals nothing else.
